grand_strategy.reading: Tuvalu's strategy is survival through recognition and treaty, not power: it keeps Taipei against Beijing's pull, binds itself to Canberra through the Falepili Union, and turns the climate case into a claim to statehood in perpetuity. Its budget rests on tuna access, which shrinks as the fish move, on a .tv lease, and on donors it cannot replace, so its freedom of action is largely borrowed. The paradox is that the treaty which keeps the state secure also needs Australia's agreement for any new security step, so the stronger the Taiwan ties become, the more Canberra's assent matters.

stances.note: Ally by treaty: the Falepili Union is a binding treaty (signed 9-10 November 2023 - the dates differ by source - in force 28 August 2024). It obliges Australia to respond when Tuvalu asks for help in a major disaster, a pandemic or military aggression, and requires Tuvalu to agree with Australia any new defence or security engagement with third parties. The ontology reads a treaty as ally. Canberra grades Tuvalu partner, because DFAT counts four alliances (US, NZ, PNG, Fiji) and Tuvalu is not one of them; the gap between the text and the list is recorded, not resolved. Bond affinity: climate and Pacific-family framing.

stances.note: Partner, not ally, for now. Recognition has been kept since Teo's government took office in February 2024: Teo told the AP in March 2024 that the ties stay, citing shared democratic values, and ruled out Beijing. His first official state visit to Taipei (November 2025) was welcomed by President Lai with a military ceremony and was reported with a treaty framework to secure statehood. The reports disagree on whether the treaty was signed (CNA: three pacts signed; AAP: planned), and no signed treaty could be confirmed in the sources read; recognition alone is a diplomatic tie, not a security alignment. Upgrade to ally if the treaty is confirmed as signed. Trend warming on the 2025 visit and the deepening language. Since 2013-03 is the Taiwan embassy's opening, the earliest dated fact in the sources read; the recognition itself is older and undated here.

stances.note: Rival, not neutral: Tuvalu keeps no ties with the PRC and holds a posture against it, not an absence of one. Beijing presses the state to switch recognition; Teo's government refused the move and the 'two-China' option in 2024, and the Taiwan tie remains the contested line (Reuters, 2019). That is a competition over one recognition, with friction and no will to destroy, which is the rival reading. No source uses the word 'rival' for this pair, so the grade rests on reporting of the contest and stays at confidence C. Bond none: interest only, no kinship or grievance. Since 2024-03 is the current government's line, the contest itself is older.

stances.note: Partner: the New Zealand-Tuvalu Statement of Partnership (3 March 2019, signed by Foreign Minister Peters and Prime Minister Sopoaga) commits both governments to work together on climate change, workforce development and regional security. It is cooperation without a treaty or an alliance, so partner rather than ally. Bond affinity: Pacific family and shared Commonwealth membership. Only one tier-1 source was read for the statement itself, hence confidence B.

stances.note: Partner: the 1979 Treaty of Friendship (ratified by the US Senate in 1983) ended the US claim to four Tuvaluan islands (Funafuti, Nukufetau, Nukulaelae, Niulakita), so it is a settlement, not a defence pact, and not an alliance. The working relationship is fisheries (the South Pacific Tuna Treaty, in force 1988, with Tuvalu as a party alongside the US and other Pacific parties) and development. The 2023 engagement could not be confirmed: the September 2023 embassy openings named the Cook Islands and Niue, not Tuvalu, and no Tuvalu-specific 2023 action was found in the sources read. Bond none: the claim is settled and the relationship is transactional. Left open for review.
